sentences.text: The case of the prosecution as outlined in the charge sheet is that the accused, fearing exposure of his illicit relationship with the deceased's mother, which she knew NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR about, and seeking vengeance for his younger brother Shasappa's death, exploited his familiarity with the victim/ deceased and on 26.9.2011 at around 6:45 p.m., he collected her near Vaibhav Theatre in Banahatti, promising to take her to the native - Asangi Village.

Instead, he took her on his motorcycle bearing No. KA-48- K-8988 to a forested area en route, where he raped her between 7:00 p.m. and 8:00 p.m., and then murdered her by strangling her neck with her veil (odni).

While investigation records suggest that certain prosecution witnesses mentioned prior enmity between the accused, the complainant, and others linked to Shasappa's demise, no such witness referenced the purported affair before the Investigating Officer.
This element appears to stem primarily from the alleged voluntary - 10 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR statement of the accused rather than independent evidence gathered.
Moreover, during trial, no one including the complainant/ PW-1, testified to this relationship.
Consequently, the prosecution has failed to establish the alleged motive.

7. The prosecution firmly maintains that on 26.09.2011 at approximately 5:30 p.m., the deceased left Smt. Ningavva's (PW-6) residence in Lakshmigudda to return home, but did not arrive at her parental home on that day.
The next morning i.e, on 27.09.2011 around 9:00 a.m., her body was found in a forested area near Dempo Dairy.

8. During their evidence, PW-1 and other prosecution witnesses, namely PWs 2 to 4 and 6 to 9,
deposed that upon reaching the spot they observed multiple injuries on the body of the deceased and formed an impression that she had been subjected to rape and subsequently murdered.
The inquest report marked at Ex. P3 and the post-mortem report marked at Ex. P20 corroborate their account.

In the post- mortem report, the medical officer opined that the cause of - 11 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR death was due to strangulation, while reserving his opinion on the question of rape pending receipt of the RFSL report.
9. The materials on record clearly reveal that the accused has not disputed any of these aspects.

Moreover, during his deposition as DW-1, the accused stated that upon learning of the deceased's Yamanappa S/O Satyappa Mang vs State Of Karnataka on 30 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49300808/
5 death, he too visited the spot and saw the body.

10. The crucial question that now arises for consideration is whether the prosecution has adduced sufficient evidence to establish the accused's involvement in the alleged crime.
It is an admitted fact that there is no eye - 12 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR witness or direct evidence to corroborate the case of the prosecution.
The prosecution, therefore, rests its case on circumstantial evidence, principally the "last seen theory" and other attendant circumstances, to support its contention.

11. In Satpal v. State of Haryana [(2018) 6 SCC 610] Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has reiterated the legal position governing the field in following words:
"...Criminal jurisprudence and the plethora of judicial precedents leave little room for reconsideration of the basic principles for invocation of the last seen theory as a facet of circumstantial evidence.

sentences.text: Succinctly stated, it may be a weak kind of evidence by itself to found conviction upon the same singularly.

But when it is coupled with other circumstances such as the time when the deceased was last seen with the accused,
and the recovery of the corpse being in very close proximity of time, the accused owes an explanation under Section 106 of the Evidence Act with regard to the circumstances under which death may have taken place.

If the accused offers no explanation, or furnishes a wrong explanation, absconds, motive is established, and there is corroborative evidence available inter alia in - 13 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR the form of recovery or otherwise forming a chain of circumstances leading to the only inference for guilt of the accused,
incompatible with any possible hypothesis of innocence, conviction can be based on the same.
If there be any doubt or break in the link of chain of circumstances, the benefit of doubt must go to the accused.
Each case will therefore have to be examined on its own facts for invocation of the doctrine...".

sentences.text: The defense has not set up a case that any such telecast, pertaining to the crime in question, was aired either before registration of the FIR or prior to the commencement of the investigation.
In the absence of any foundational material in that regard, the mere fact that PW5 is stated to have seen a television show cannot, by itself, render his testimony unsafe.

17. Nevertheless, if the suggestion put to PW5 on behalf of the accused is properly construed, it in fact proceeds on the premise that there was a telecast showing the accused taking a girl on a motorcycle on the relevant day.
Such a suggestion amounts to a clear implied admission on the part of the defense that it was the accused who had taken the deceased on a motorcycle.

Once that suggestion is accepted, the necessary inference is that there existed a video recording depicting the accused taking away the deceased on a motorcycle and that the accused does not dispute the correctness of such depiction in the telecast.

18. Further, even if one were to proceed on the basis of - 17 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR the suggestion made on behalf of the accused that a report concerning the incident was telecast on the very next day and that PW5 visited the police station only on the following day to make his statement, the contention does not withstand scrutiny.
If that version is accepted, PW5 would have given his statement before the police two days after the incident.

However, the contemporaneous material on record, particularly the inquest report marked as Ex. P3, establishes that the inquest was conducted at the spot on 27.09.2011 between 1:30 p.m.
and 3:30 p.m., during the course of which PW5 disclosed the aforesaid facts to the police and to the other persons present.

The documentary evidence thus clearly demonstrates that PW5 had furnished the relevant information at the earliest available opportunity, which belies the defense theory of a delayed and prompted statement.
In view of this, the Court is unable to accept the contention of the accused and finds no merit in the challenge to the credibility of PW5's statement.

It is well-settled that the "last seen"
doctrine gains potency in cases of such brief lapses, particularly when embedded within an unbroken chain of circumstances.

21. It is a well-established principle that in cases founded upon circumstantial evidence, the prosecution bears the burden of proving each individual circumstance and the interlinking nexus among them beyond reasonable doubt.

The cumulative effect of these circumstances must constitute a complete and consistent chain, leaving no reasonable ground to conclude otherwise than that within all human probability; the offence was perpetrated by the accused.
In this context, it becomes necessary for this Court to carefully examine the remaining links in the chain of circumstances that collectively point toward the culpability of the accused.

For these reasons, this Court is of the view that the trial court rightly held the accused guilty of the murder of the deceased based on the "last seen" theory supported by - 24 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR other corroborative circumstantial evidence.
27. Learned Counsel for the Accused has strenuously contended that the prosecution has failed to establish the commission of rape upon the deceased.

In support of this submission, reliance has been placed on the RFSL report marked as Ex. P26, which records that seminal stains were not detected on any of the garments said to belong to the deceased or the accused, nor in the anal or vaginal swabs collected during investigation.
28. It is true that as per the RFSL report no seminal stains were detected on any of the aforesaid articles seized and preserved during the course of investigation.
However, in the considered view of this Court, the said circumstance alone cannot be treated as conclusive to determine whether rape was committed.
At this juncture, it is appropriate to refer to the definition of 'rape' under Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code.
As per clause (a) of the said provision, penetration of the penis into the vagina to any extent is sufficient to constitute the offence of rape.
It is true that as per the RFSL report, no seminal stains were detected on any of the articles seized or preserved during the investigation of the present case.
However, in the considered view of this Court, the said circumstance by itself cannot be treated as a decisive or conclusive factor to determine whether the offence of rape was committed or not.
The legal position is well settled that the absence of semen or spermatozoa does not, in law, negate the possibility of rape if there is otherwise cogent and reliable evidence indicating penetration.
30. At this juncture, it becomes apposite to advert to the definition of the offence of rape as contained in Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code.

Under clause (a) of Section 375 IPC, a man is said to commit rape if he "penetrates his penis, to any extent, into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her to do so with him or any other person."

Thus, even the slightest penetration to any extent is sufficient to constitute the offence, and proof of ejaculation or presence - 26 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR of seminal stains is not a statutory requirement for attracting Section 375 IPC.

sentences.text: In the present case, PW22 - Dr. Sunitha Naik, one of the doctors who conducted the post-mortem examination on the deceased, has unequivocally deposed that the post- mortem examination revealed bite marks on both cheeks of the deceased along with nail scratches in the inguinal region, thigh proximate to the genitals, left shoulder and neck, and that all those injuries were consistent with the perpetration of rape.
She has further stated that the hymen of the deceased was found ruptured, accompanied by haemorrhage resulting from such rupture.
This evidence tendered by PW22 stands in complete harmony with the ocular accounts furnished by the prosecution witnesses who viewed the cadaver at the crime scene.

These witnesses have testified before the Court regarding the observed haemorrhage from the victim's private part, alongside additional external injuries and signs indicative of sexual assault upon the deceased.

These reports assert that upon subjecting the accused to meticulous oral examination, radiographic imaging (X-ray), and bite mark scrutiny, the resultant analysis correlated the accused's dental patterns with the bite wound on the deceased's left cheek.
The prosecution has examined the doctor who authored these reports as PW-23.
Thus, the cumulative effect of the aforementioned materials on record furnishes ample basis to hold that the accused committed rape upon the deceased, as alleged by the prosecution.

33. Learned Counsel for the Accused has made a faint attempt to discredit the prosecution's version by pointing to minor inconsistencies in the evidence and certain procedural lapses during investigation.
One such instance relates to a reference made by PW-8 to one "Prakash Mang" as the person who allegedly took the victim girl on the motorcycle.
A careful reading of the deposition of PW-8 clearly establishes - 28 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR that he is a hearsay witness, and the said statement was not based on his personal knowledge.
Moreover, the portion of his deposition found at page 2 indicates that such a mention is nothing but an inadvertent and typographical error rather than a substantive statement made by the witness.

34. The defense has also questioned the reliability of the post-mortem report marked as Ex.P20,
contending that being a partial report and that it cannot be relied upon.
This contention is devoid of merit.
The record reveals that Ex.P20 was prepared based on the actual findings observed during the post-mortem examination.
It remained partial only to the limited extent of the alleged sexual assault aspect, which was kept pending till receipt of the RFSL report.
The medical experts had rightly awaited the RFSL findings before forming a conclusive opinion regarding the commission of rape on the deceased.

sentences.text: Another contention raised by the accused is that he did not abscond after the alleged incident and was present even during the spot mahazar.
As discussed earlier, PW-12 - 29 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR Sri Sangappa has testified that he visited the scene of occurrence along with the accused.
At the same time, he has categorically stated that the accused remained at the spot only for about 10 to 15 minutes after their arrival and thereafter left the place.
This part of his testimony remained unshaken in cross-examination as no effort was made by the defense to challenge or contradict it.

Further, though while deposing as DW-1, the accused claimed that he had visited the police station several times with the complainant and PW- 7 and was present during the spot mahazar, no suggestion to that effect was put to PW-1, PW-7, or any other prosecution witness.
Hence, the plea of the accused regarding his continued presence in the locality after his name surfaced as the person last seen with the deceased remains unsupported by any credible evidence.
Consequently, this Court finds no substance in the said contention.

36. Learned Counsel for the Accused has even pointed out similar other instances such as the four-hour delay in forwarding the FIR to the jurisdictional magistrate, the - 30 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR inordinate two-month lag in submitting the post-mortem report, the omission to collect blood samples and nail scrapings from both the deceased and the accused, and the failure to secure documents substantiating ownership of the motorcycle in question, etc.
No doubt, such minor discrepancies and the lapses do exist in the case.

However, they pale into insignificance against the backdrop of the unimpeachable and incontrovertible evidence,
compounded by the accused's inability to furnish any plausible explanation for proximity to the deceased shortly before her demise, the blood stains on his shirt, the injuries on his person, etc.
This Court is therefore constrained to hold that these discrepancies or shortcomings are too insignificant to displace the substantial proof adduced by the prosecution.
37. It is also pertinent to observe that the accused hails from the same community as the complainant and the deceased, and all are residents of the same locality.

Admittedly, no enmity or ill-will subsisted between the accused and any prosecution witness, furnishing no motive - 31 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR for any of them to depose falsely before the Court.
Consequently, the hypothesis of false implication of the accused stands wholly ruled out.

The accused, in his testimony, has leveled no allegation against any of the prosecution witness regarding his fabricated involvement, save a bald assertion that the police implicated him merely to parade someone as the perpetrator.
In light of the incriminating materials available on record, this Court finds the above contention of the accused is utterly bereft of merit.

sentences.text: The robust evidence on record establishes that the accused was last seen in the company of the deceased on 26.09.2011 around 6:30 PM, reinforced suggestive indication of rape upon her, the unexplained injuries on his person, and the brief interval between their last sighting together and the discovery of her corpse.
If these factors are blend together, it would forge an unbroken chain of circumstances unerringly pointing to the accused's culpability.
The materials on record sufficiently substantiate rape or an attempt thereof, warranting presumption of the underlying impetus for the - 32 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR offence.
Accordingly, this Court holds that the accused has failed to demonstrate any tenable basis for unsettling the impugned judgment, as urged in the appeal.
39. The present case concerns the rape and murder of a 15-year-old girl, who unsuspectingly accompanied the accused on the fateful day, believing his assurance of taking her to her native place.

The Trial Court, while imposing sentence under the impugned judgment, awarded life imprisonment to the accused for the offenses punishable under Sections 376 and 302 of the Indian Penal Code and further directed him to pay a fine of Rs.25,000/- for each offence.
Upon a careful consideration of the evidence and the reasoning assigned by the Trial Court, we find no justifiable ground to interfere with the sentence so imposed.
40. Under the impugned judgment, the Trial Court has further directed that out of the total fine amount of Rs.50,000/- a sum of Rs.40,000/- shall be paid to the complainant by way of compensation.

However, it is noticed that the Trial Court did not invoke the provisions of Section - 33 - NC: 2026:KHC-D:1335-DB HC-KAR 357A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, notwithstanding the fact that the judgment was rendered on 11.12.2020.

It is true that the offence in question was committed on 26.09.2011 and Section 357A Cr.P.C. came be inserted pursuant to the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2008, which came into force on 31.12.2009.

This omission,
however, does not preclude this Court from making an appropriate recommendation.

Considering the overall circumstances of the case and the plight of the victim's family, we deem it just and proper to recommend to the District Legal Services Authority, Bagalkot, to assess and determine suitable compensation payable to the parents of the deceased/victim and to ensure prompt disbursement of the same in accordance with the Victim Compensation Scheme framed under Section 357A Cr.P.C.
41.

In the result, this court proceeds to pass the following:
ORDER i) Appeal is dismissed.
